source: បច្ចេកទេស ដាំដុះដំណាំដំឡូងជ្វា (Sweet Potato Cultivation Techniques), MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture, 2018
text:
Sweetpotato weevil, Cylas formicarius (Fabricius) (order Coleoptera, family Brentidae), is described in this source as one of the most damaging pests of sweet potato wherever the crop is grown, occurring widely across tropical growing regions including tropical America and Asia, and considered a serious problem in Cambodia.

Adults have an ant-like appearance (hence the species name 'formicarius'): a dark blue-black body with reddish-orange legs, head, and a long snout, roughly 5-8mm long. Females can lay on the order of 100-200 eggs over their lifetime, typically into cracks or wounds on exposed tubers. Larvae are legless, cream/white, curved grubs that tunnel inside tubers and vine bases, feeding internally.

Damage: larval tunneling in tubers and vine bases weakens plants and directly damages tubers; the plant's defensive response to tunneling produces bitter-tasting terpenoid compounds in the damaged tissue, rendering affected tubers unpalatable and unmarketable even when the visible damage is limited.

Management measures given: field sanitation (removing crop residue that harbors weevils); crop rotation, avoiding repeated sweet potato planting in the same field; using only clean, pest-free vine cuttings for planting; hilling/mounding soil over the tubers to reduce adult access for egg-laying; harvesting promptly rather than leaving mature tubers in the ground, since soil cracking from drying exposes tubers to weevil attack; pre-plant treatment by soaking cuttings in insecticide for about 30 minutes to control eggs/larvae present on the cutting; and, where infestation is found, chemical control with an example active ingredient named in the source as Bensultap, with the source describing a first application around one month after planting and a possible second application about one month after the first if needed. Pheromone traps are also mentioned as a monitoring/control option.
